newsitem.title: KENYA: World Bank says Africa must aim at 10 pct growth.
newsitem.headline: World Bank says Africa must aim at 10 pct growth.

text.p: World Bank Vice-President Callisto Madavo said on Thursday African economies must aim at 10 percent annual growth to eradicate crippling poverty.

With population growth averaging around 3.0 percent it was not good enough for African countries to aim at annual gross domestic product (GDP) growth levels of 4.0 to 5.0 percent because that would not sustain development, Madavo told a news conference.
"African countries need to aim at around eight to 10 percent. Then real growth will take off," he said after four days of meetings in the Kenyan capital Nairobi.
Madavo said a new crop of African leaders preoccupied with empowering their people pointed the way forward to continued economic growth in coming years.
Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki and Mali's President Alpha Oumar Konare exemplified the new leadership.
"A new leadership is emerging on the scene and (it) is really focused on economic development," Madavo said. "There is a new platform emerging on which African peoples can build."
"The new leaders have a focus around economic development and poverty alleviation," he said.
Africa's average GDP rose to around 5.6 percent in 1996 from about 1.0 percent in 1991 and there was potential for further growth this year, he said.
The World Bank, the International Monetary Fund or donor countries could not take credit for Africa's economic turnabout because "credit must belong to the people".

"Africa is on the move. There are a number of developments, such as democratic opening up, political stability, elections and the involvement of ordinary people in political and economic life in Africa which augurs well for the future."
He said despite Kenya's relative stability it had the potential to do better and action was required on a number of poorly implemented World Bank-funded projects.
The economies of Uganda and Tanzania were in relative terms performing better than Kenya's and Kenyan people must ask themselves why, he said.
